summary: Sort intervals by start time, then sweep once to merge overlaps or insert a new interval in place.
lesson: Interval problems become easy once you sort by start time -- after that, checking whether two intervals overlap or merging a run of overlapping intervals is just a single left-to-right sweep. The core comparison is: does this interval's start fall before (or at) the end of the interval you're currently building? If so, extend the current interval's end; if not, start a new one. Because the hard part (establishing an order) is handled by the sort, the sweep itself only needs to look at the interval immediately before it -- no backtracking required. This is why interval problems (merging, inserting, meeting-room conflicts) all end up with roughly the same shape: sort, then one pass.
recognize_when: input is a list of [start, end] ranges
asking to merge, insert, or find overlapping intervals
need to find free/busy time gaps
'overlap' or 'conflict' appears in the problem statement

complexity.notes: dominated by the sort; the merge sweep itself is O(n)

gotchas: forgetting to sort first (or sorting by end instead of start)
using < instead of <= when checking overlap, mishandling touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3]
mutating the input list's inner lists when tuples were expected, or not copying before mutating
